title: Janhvi Kapoor Liked a Post Calling Peddi the 'Most Expensive Disrespect' to Its Leading Woman. Then She Unliked It.
excerpt: A viral screenshot has turned a ₹350-crore sports drama's treatment of its female lead into a national conversation about consent, creative control, and the gap between what an actress questions and what a director keeps.
body:
Ram Charan's Peddi opened to ₹112 crore worldwide on Day 1, the biggest Telugu opening of 2026. But the conversation that has dominated social media since release day has nothing to do with the box office.

An Instagram post from a page called Recommendation Community went viral on June 4 with a title that has since become the controversy's shorthand: "Peddi: The Most Expensive Disrespect Ever Paid to a Leading Woman in Indian Cinema." The post argued that the ₹350-crore sports drama frames the denial of human identity as a systemic evil while denying its female lead, Achiyamma, the same humanity. It criticised close-up shots of her midriff and body, scenes that viewers said romanticise actions without consent, and a character arc that gives Ram Charan's Peddi a sociopolitical crusade while giving Janhvi Kapoor a glamour reel.

Then eagle-eyed fans noticed something: the post was liked by Janhvi Kapoor herself.

The Like, the Unlike, and the Silence

The like is no longer visible. Multiple users confirmed that Kapoor appears to have unliked the post after screenshots circulated. Neither Kapoor nor the filmmakers have issued an official response. But the damage — or the signal, depending on how you read it — was already done.

The post's central claim is pointed: reports indicate that Janhvi Kapoor explicitly questioned certain shots during post-production, a boundary that mirrors her recent public stance against oversexualisation. In an April 2026 interview on the Raj Shamani Podcast, she said: "Zooming into body parts without consent is invasive. Even if we dress a certain way, we're not expecting someone to zoom in on specific body parts." She drew a distinction between performance and exploitation, citing her own work on the song Bheegi Saadi as an example of consensual sensuality versus the non-consensual kind.

The viral post took that distinction and applied it directly to Peddi: "She drew a professional line, but the final edit kept the footage anyway. This isn't a case of an actress failing to stand up for herself. It is a director choosing to ignore a boundary because he decided her consent mattered less than his box office numbers."

The Backlash Has Two Sides

The reaction online has split along familiar lines. One camp argues that Kapoor chose to sign the film, read the script, and showed up on set — liking a post that criticises the very project she participated in strikes them as disingenuous. "You could've said NO," wrote one widely shared reply. "You read the script and signed it, so don't play victim now."

The other camp points out that a signed contract is not blanket consent. Post-production editing, camera angles chosen without the actor's input, and final cuts that override an actress's stated objections are the norm, not the exception, in a star-driven industry where creative control belongs to the director and producer. What a woman can do when power is asymmetrical from the start is a question that extends well beyond one film.

The Bigger Conversation

What started as speculation around a social media like has evolved into a wider conversation about female representation in mainstream commercial cinema. Multiple viewers pointed out that Peddi — marketed as a family-friendly, inspirational sports drama about a village fighting for recognition — undercuts its own messaging by reducing its female lead to a set of visual markers while its male lead gets narrative depth.

Reddit and X have been filled with comments noting the pattern: Telugu and Hindi commercial cinema regularly casts its heroines as accessories to the hero's journey, where their function is to look good, be won, and occasionally be rescued. The criticism is not new. What is new is the leading actress appearing to agree with it in real time.

For diaspora audiences watching from abroad, the episode is a reminder that the Indian film industry's relationship with its women — onscreen and off — remains unsettled. The conversation about who gets to decide what a female body means on camera is not over. Peddi's box office will keep climbing. So will the questions it raised.
